content_html:
Not all those who wander are lost.

– J.R.R. Tolkien

Today I’m happy to announce Flycheck 38 - easily the biggest and most ambitious Flycheck release since I took over the stewardship of the project. It’s the release where Flycheck grows a proper story for language servers, gets the kind of inline diagnostics you’d expect from a modern editor, and learns to apply fixes - all without giving up the checker model that made it popular in the first place.

The version number, I’ll admit, doesn’t do this one justice - it’s just the next integer after 37, and nothing about “38” whispers “special”. But that’s how it goes with version numbers: some releases are more special than others, and you’d rarely guess which from the number alone.

There and back again

A little history, because it’s what makes me this excited. Flycheck was born to give Emacs a genuinely modern linting experience, back when the built-in options were, let’s charitably say, uninspiring. For years it was the way to get on-the-fly checking in Emacs. But then development slowed to a crawl, Flymake got a ground-up rewrite and quietly caught up in a lot of areas - it even grew end-of-line diagnostics recently - and I started seeing people wonder aloud whether Flycheck still brought anything to the table.

I get the question - a stagnant project invites it. But I never believed Flycheck was done; it was just resting. This release is my answer: proof that it can still innovate and still delight. And I’m genuinely grateful for the competition. Flymake pushing hard is exactly what nudged me to think bigger and bolder than another round of bugfixes. Competition in this space is a good thing, full stop - it makes both projects better and Emacs users the winners. If you’re curious how the two stack up now, the manual keeps an honest side-by-side.

So, in the spirit of boldly going where many editors have gone before, here’s what’s new.

Eglot support, finally built in

For years the story around Flycheck and LSP was awkward. Eglot renders its diagnostics through Flymake and offers no Flycheck backend of its own, so if you wanted your LSP errors in Flycheck’s error list you had to reach for the third-party flycheck-eglot package. It worked, but “install another package to bridge two things that ship with Emacs” never sat right with me.

Flycheck now bridges that gap itself. Enable global-flycheck-eglot-mode and an Eglot-managed buffer reports the server’s diagnostics through Flycheck - the error list, the navigation, the fringe, all of it - while Eglot keeps doing the LSP heavy lifting. This obsoletes the flycheck-eglot package.1

And because Flycheck reads the raw LSP diagnostic rather than the flattened Flymake one, the bridge surfaces things Flymake-over-Eglot drops on the floor: an LSP quickfix code action becomes a Flycheck fix you can apply with C-c ! f, and a diagnostic’s related locations become navigable.

Beautiful inline diagnostics

The other thing I really wanted was inline messages - errors shown right next to the code they refer to, the way VS Code’s Error Lens, Neovim, Helix and Zed all do it. Flycheck 38 ships this out of the box.

Turn on flycheck-annotate-mode and you get it. There are two layouts - a compact eol message after the line, and a roomy below layout that lays the full messages out on their own lines underneath, with connectors pointing at the offending column. By default the line at point gets the roomy treatment while the rest stay compact, so the error you’re working on is spelled out in full without every other line shouting for attention. There’s also an Error Lens-style whole-line background tint and a right-aligned sideline style if that’s your thing - the manual has a shot of each.

Turn it on everywhere with the global mode:

(global-flycheck-annotate-mode 1)
;; optional: the Error Lens-style whole-line tint
(setq flycheck-annotate-background t)

A word on the name, since it’s a funny little story. I’d have loved to call this flycheck-inline-mode, but that name was taken by the (now deprecated) flycheck-inline package. “Diagnostics” was the other obvious choice, except Flycheck has always called them errors, not diagnostics - flycheck-error, the error list, flycheck-checkers - and I didn’t want to introduce a second vocabulary for the same thing. So flycheck-annotate-mode it is. Naming things is (still) hard.

Native LSP support, no client required

And to top things off: Flycheck can now talk to a language server directly - no Eglot, no lsp-mode, no full LSP client at all.

Here’s the itch this scratches. A growing number of linters ship their own LSP server - RuboCop, Ruff, Biome, Harper and friends - and a traditional command checker spawns the linter afresh on every check, paying its startup cost over and over (anyone who’s waited on rubocop loading a big project knows the feeling). The linter’s own LSP server stays resident and lints incrementally instead, so checks are much snappier - and you get that without running a full language server and client just to see some diagnostics.

Enable global-flycheck-lsp-mode and it works out of the box for RuboCop (Ruby), Ruff (Python), Biome (JavaScript, TypeScript, JSON, CSS) and Harper (Markdown prose). Each server is only started if its program is installed, so turning the mode on globally is safe. Want a different one? It’s a one-liner:

;; Standard instead of RuboCop for Ruby
(setf (alist-get 'ruby-mode flycheck-lsp-servers) '("standardrb" "--lsp"))

The whole thing is built on Emacs’ own jsonrpc library, so there’s no new dependency. And where the server offers them - RuboCop’s autocorrects, Ruff’s and Biome’s quickfixes - those show up as Flycheck fixes too. It’s meant for the diagnostics-only case; when you want a full language server with completion and hover, run it through Eglot and use flycheck-eglot-mode. The manual has a table to help you pick.

Project-wide diagnostics

Flycheck has always been a resolutely buffer-local affair: it checks the file you’re looking at and shows you those errors. That’s great right up until you want the bigger picture - every problem across the files you have open, plus the cross-file errors that checkers like tsc, cargo check and mypy genuinely know about but the per-buffer view quietly throws away.

Press P in the error list and it flips to a project-wide scope: errors aggregated across every open Flycheck buffer, with those cross-file diagnostics finally given somewhere to live. It’s the closest Flycheck has come to a “problems” panel, and it’s quickly become one of my favourite things to actually use day to day.

Notice the models.py type error in there: it was reported while checking api.py, and the old per-buffer view would have dropped it on the floor. The [project] tag in the mode line tells you you’re looking at the whole project rather than a single file.

Checking remote files over TRAMP

This one is simple to describe and was honestly overdue: Flycheck now runs checkers over TRAMP. Open a file on a remote host and the checker runs there, on the remote machine, against the real environment - where before it simply refused to run at all. If you edit code on servers or inside containers over TRAMP, this alone might be worth the upgrade.

And plenty more

The three headliners above lean on a lot of supporting work that landed in the same release. The highlights:

  • Flycheck can apply fixes now. C-c ! f (flycheck-fix-error-at-point) applies the machine-applicable fix a checker suggested, C-c ! F applies every fix in the buffer at once as a single undoable change, and fixable errors get a distinct fringe indicator - a little “fix available” lightbulb. eslint --fix, cargo clippy’s suggestions, ruff, shellcheck and any SARIF-based checker carry these fixes, which Flycheck used to parse and throw away.
  • The error list got a serious overhaul: group errors by file, checker or level (and combine those dimensions), collapse the groups, and drive it all with the mouse via a strip at the top.
  • Errors can carry secondary locations - the earlier definition behind a redefinition, the borrow behind a Rust lifetime error. Jump to them with C-c ! j, and they show up after the message inline and in the error list.
  • A running check is interrupted when a newer one starts (unless it’s already made real progress), so a slow checker no longer makes Flycheck feel sluggish, and the error list no longer rescans all its rows on every cursor move.

There’s more in the changelog, but that’s the shape of it.

Putting it all together

If you want the full modern setup - on-the-fly checking everywhere, inline diagnostics, and your LSP server’s diagnostics flowing through Flycheck - here’s a use-package block that turns it all on:

(use-package flycheck
  :ensure t
  :hook ((after-init . global-flycheck-mode)
         ;; Show diagnostics inline, next to the code (Error Lens style)
         (after-init . global-flycheck-annotate-mode))
  :config
  ;; Report Eglot's LSP diagnostics through Flycheck
  (global-flycheck-eglot-mode 1))

Prefer to skip Eglot and read diagnostics straight from a linter’s own LSP server (RuboCop, Ruff, Biome, Harper)? Swap that last line for (global-flycheck-lsp-mode 1) instead. Reach for the native checker when all you want is diagnostics, and the Eglot bridge when you also want a full language server’s completion and hover.

Upgrading

Most setups will just keep working. The one thing to watch: the built-in flycheck-eglot-mode reuses the names of the old third-party flycheck-eglot package, so if you have that installed, uninstall it before relying on the built-in mode - otherwise the two define the same commands and clash.

A word on funding

Let me get a little uncomfortably candid here. In the couple of years I’ve been maintaining Flycheck, its OpenCollective has taken in less than $300 - total. Individual donations haven’t exactly moved the needle either. I’m not saying this to guilt anyone; it’s just the everyday reality of open source. Popular projects are a lot of work, and the usual reward is the quiet satisfaction of using something you helped make a bit better.

Still, if Flycheck saves you time - especially if it does so at work - please consider chipping in through OpenCollective, GitHub Sponsors, or any of the other options linked from the README. Even a small recurring amount, multiplied across the people who lean on this thing every day, would make a real difference to how much time I can put into it.

Closing thoughts

Even the smallest person can change the course of the future.

– Galadriel

When I took over Flycheck, my motivation was simple: keep the project alive, and keep the competition in this corner of Emacs going. For a long stretch that meant little more than keeping the lights on. This release is the first time in a while it’s genuinely moved forward in a big way, and I’m proud of where it landed - modern diagnostics UX, first-class LSP support in two flavours, project-wide diagnostics, and fixes, all while staying true to the checker model people love it for. Call it the return of the Jedi. I hope you’ll agree I’ve been at least modestly successful at what I set out to do.

Huge thanks to everyone who tested, reported and nudged this along. Give flycheck-annotate-mode and flycheck-lsp-mode a spin and let me know what you think.

Keep hacking!

blocks.html_en: For years the story around Flycheck and LSP was awkward. Eglot renders its diagnostics through Flymake and offers no Flycheck backend of its own, so if you wanted your LSP errors in Flycheck’s error list you had to reach for the third-party flycheck-eglot package. It worked, but “install another package to bridge two things that ship with Emacs” never sat right with me.

sentences.en: For years the story around Flycheck and LSP was awkward.
sentences.zh: 多年来，围绕 Flycheck 和 LSP 的故事一直很尴尬。

sentences.en: Eglot renders its diagnostics through Flymake and offers no Flycheck backend of its own, so if you wanted your LSP errors in Flycheck’s error list you had to reach for the third-party flycheck-eglot package.
sentences.zh: Eglot 通过 Flymake 呈现其诊断，并且不提供自己的 Flycheck 后端，因此如果您希望在 Flycheck 的错误列表中显示 LSP 错误，则必须使用第三方 Flycheck-eglot 包。

sentences.en: It worked, but “install another package to bridge two things that ship with Emacs” never sat right with me.
sentences.zh: 它确实有效，但“安装另一个包来桥接 Emacs 附带的两个东西”对我来说并不合适。

blocks.html_en: Flycheck now bridges that gap itself. Enable global-flycheck-eglot-mode and an Eglot-managed buffer reports the server’s diagnostics through Flycheck - the error list, the navigation, the fringe, all of it - while Eglot keeps doing the LSP heavy lifting. This obsoletes the flycheck-eglot package.1

sentences.en: Flycheck now bridges that gap itself.
sentences.zh: Flycheck 现在弥补了这一差距。

sentences.en: Enable global-flycheck-eglot-mode and an Eglot-managed buffer reports the server’s diagnostics through Flycheck - the error list, the navigation, the fringe, all of it - while Eglot keeps doing the LSP heavy lifting.
sentences.zh: 启用 global-flycheck-eglot-mode ，Eglot 管理的缓冲区通过 Flycheck 报告服务器的诊断信息 - 错误列表、导航、边缘，所有这些 - 而 Eglot 则继续承担 LSP 的繁重工作。

sentences.zh: 这会废弃 Flycheck-eglot 包。1

blocks.html_en: Turn on flycheck-annotate-mode and you get it. There are two layouts - a compact eol message after the line, and a roomy below layout that lays the full messages out on their own lines underneath, with connectors pointing at the offending column. By default the line at point gets the roomy treatment while the rest stay compact, so the error you’re working on is spelled out in full without every other line shouting for attention. There’s also an Error Lens-style whole-line background tint and a right-aligned sideline style if that’s your thing - the manual has a shot of each.

blocks.html_en: Here’s the itch this scratches. A growing number of linters ship their own LSP server - RuboCop, Ruff, Biome, Harper and friends - and a traditional command checker spawns the linter afresh on every check, paying its startup cost over and over (anyone who’s waited on rubocop loading a big project knows the feeling). The linter’s own LSP server stays resident and lints incrementally instead, so checks are much snappier - and you get that without running a full language server and client just to see some diagnostics.

blocks.html_en: Flycheck has always been a resolutely buffer-local affair: it checks the file you’re looking at and shows you those errors. That’s great right up until you want the bigger picture - every problem across the files you have open, plus the cross-file errors that checkers like tsc, cargo check and mypy genuinely know about but the per-buffer view quietly throws away.

sentences.en: Flycheck has always been a resolutely buffer-local affair: it checks the file you’re looking at and shows you those errors.
sentences.zh: Flycheck 始终是一个绝对缓冲区本地事务：它检查您正在查看的文件并显示这些错误。

sentences.en: That’s great right up until you want the bigger picture - every problem across the files you have open, plus the cross-file errors that checkers like tsc, cargo check and mypy genuinely know about but the per-buffer view quietly throws away.
sentences.zh: 这很好，直到您想要了解更大的情况 - 您打开的文件中的每个问题，加上 tsc、cargo check 和 mypy 等检查器真正了解的跨文件错误，但每个缓冲区视图都会悄悄地丢弃。

blocks.html_en: Press P in the error list and it flips to a project-wide scope: errors aggregated across every open Flycheck buffer, with those cross-file diagnostics finally given somewhere to live. It’s the closest Flycheck has come to a “problems” panel, and it’s quickly become one of my favourite things to actually use day to day.

blocks.html_en: This one is simple to describe and was honestly overdue: Flycheck now runs checkers over TRAMP. Open a file on a remote host and the checker runs there, on the remote machine, against the real environment - where before it simply refused to run at all. If you edit code on servers or inside containers over TRAMP, this alone might be worth the upgrade.

blocks.html_en: • Flycheck can apply fixes now. C-c ! f (flycheck-fix-error-at-point) applies the machine-applicable fix a checker suggested, C-c ! sentences.en: A running check is interrupted when a newer one starts (unless it’s already made real progress), so a slow checker no longer makes Flycheck feel sluggish, and the error list no longer rescans all its rows on every cursor move.

content_html_zh:
并非所有徘徊的人都迷失了方向。 – J.R.R. 托尔金

今天，我很高兴地宣布 Flycheck 38——这是我接手该项目以来规模最大、最雄心勃勃的 Flycheck 版本。 在这个版本中，Flycheck 为语言服务器开发了一个合适的故事，获得了您期望从现代编辑器中获得的内联诊断，并学会应用修复 - 所有这些都没有放弃最初使其流行的检查器模型。

我承认，版本号并不能公正地体现这一点——它只是 37 之后的下一个整数，“38”没有任何“特殊”的意思。 但这就是版本号的情况：有些版本比其他版本更特别，你很难仅从版本号中猜出哪个版本。

那里又回来

一点历史，因为它让我如此兴奋。 Flycheck 的诞生是为了给 Emacs 带来真正现代的 linting 体验，而那时内置选项（让我们宽容地说）平淡无奇。 多年来，这是在 Emacs 中进行即时检查的方式。 但后来开发速度慢了下来，Flymake 进行了彻底的重写，并悄悄地赶上了很多领域——它最近甚至增加了行尾诊断——我开始看到人们大声怀疑 Flycheck 是否仍然带来了任何东西。

我明白了这个问题——一个停滞不前的项目引发了它。 但我从不相信 Flycheck 已经完成了；它只是在休息。 这个版本就是我的答案：证明它仍然可以创新并且仍然令人愉悦。 我真的很感谢这次比赛。 Flymake 的大力推动正是促使我思考比另一轮错误修复更大、更大胆的原因。 这个领域的竞争是一件好事，句号 - 它使两个项目变得更好，并使 Emacs 用户成为赢家。 如果你好奇这两者现在如何叠加，手册会诚实地并列说明。

因此，本着大胆尝试许多编辑以前做过的事情的精神，以下是新内容。

Eglot 支持，终于内置了

多年来，围绕 Flycheck 和 LSP 的故事一直很尴尬。 Eglot 通过 Flymake 呈现其诊断，并且不提供自己的 Flycheck 后端，因此如果您希望在 Flycheck 的错误列表中显示 LSP 错误，则必须使用第三方 Flycheck-eglot 包。 它确实有效，但“安装另一个包来桥接 Emacs 附带的两个东西”对我来说并不合适。

Flycheck 现在弥补了这一差距。 启用 global-flycheck-eglot-mode ，Eglot 管理的缓冲区通过 Flycheck 报告服务器的诊断信息 - 错误列表、导航、边缘，所有这些 - 而 Eglot 则继续承担 LSP 的繁重工作。 这会废弃 Flycheck-eglot 包。1

由于 Flycheck 读取的是原始 LSP 诊断信息，而不是扁平化的 Flymake 诊断信息，因此桥接器会显示 Flymake-over-Eglot 掉落在地板上的东西：LSP 快速修复代码操作会变成 Flycheck 修复，您可以使用 C-c 来应用！ f，并且诊断的相关位置变得可导航。

漂亮的在线诊断

我真正想要的另一件事是内联消息 - 错误显示在它们引用的代码旁边，就像 VS Code 的 Error Lens、Neovim、Helix 和 Zed 所做的那样。 Flycheck 38 开箱即用。

打开 Flycheck-annotate-mode 就可以了。 有两种布局 - 行后紧凑的 eol 消息，以及宽敞的下方布局，将完整消息放在下面自己的行上，连接器指向有问题的列。 默认情况下，该点的行得到宽敞的处理，而其余的行保持紧凑，因此您正在处理的错误会被完整地拼写出来，而不会引起其他所有行的注意。 如果您喜欢的话，还有错误镜头式的全线背景色调和右对齐的边线样式 - 手册中都有相应的镜头。

使用全局模式在任何地方打开它：

(global-flycheck-annotate-mode 1)
;; optional: the Error Lens-style whole-line tint
(setq flycheck-annotate-background t)

名字上有一个词，因为这是一个有趣的小故事。 我很想将其称为“flycheck-inline-mode”，但该名称是由（现已弃用的）flycheck-inline 包使用的。 “诊断”是另一个明显的选择，除了 Flycheck 总是称它们为错误，而不是诊断——flycheck-error、错误列表、flycheck-checkers——而且我不想为同一件事引入第二个词汇。 所以它就是 Flycheck-annotate-mode。 命名事物（仍然）很困难。

原生LSP支持，无需客户端

最重要的是：Flycheck 现在可以直接与语言服务器对话 - 没有 Eglot，没有 lsp 模式，根本没有完整的 LSP 客户端。

这就是抓伤的痒处。 越来越多的 linter 发布了自己的 LSP 服务器 - RuboCop、Ruff、Biome、Harper 和朋友 - 传统的命令检查器在每次检查时重新生成 linter，一遍又一遍地支付其启动成本（任何等待 rubocop 加载大型项目的人都知道这种感觉）。 linter 自己的 LSP 服务器保持常驻并增量地进行 lint，因此检查更加快捷 - 并且您无需运行完整的语言服务器和客户端来查看一些诊断信息即可获得这一点。

启用 global-flycheck-lsp-mode，它可以开箱即用地用于 RuboCop (Ruby)、Ruff (Python)、Biome（JavaScript、TypeScript、JSON、CSS）和 Harper（Markdown 散文）。 每个服务器仅在安装了其程序后才会启动，因此全局打开该模式是安全的。 想要一件不同的吗？ 这是一行：

;; Standard instead of RuboCop for Ruby
(setf (alist-get 'ruby-mode flycheck-lsp-servers) '("standardrb" "--lsp"))

整个事情都是建立在 Emacs 自己的 jsonrpc 库之上，因此没有新的依赖项。 服务器提供的地方 - RuboCop 的自动更正、Ruff 和 Biome 的快速修复 - 这些也显示为 Flycheck 修复。 它仅适用于诊断情况；当您想要一个具有补全和悬停功能的完整语言服务器时，请通过 Eglot 运行它并使用 Flycheck-eglot-mode。 手册上有一个表格可以帮助您选择。

项目范围的诊断

Flycheck 始终是一个绝对缓冲区本地事务：它检查您正在查看的文件并显示这些错误。 这很好，直到您想要了解更大的情况 - 您打开的文件中的每个问题，加上 tsc、cargo check 和 mypy 等检查器真正了解的跨文件错误，但每个缓冲区视图都会悄悄地丢弃。

在错误列表中按 P，它会翻转到项目范围内的范围：错误在每个打开的 Flycheck 缓冲区中聚合，这些跨文件诊断最终得到了生存的地方。 这是 Flycheck 中最接近“问题”面板的工具，它很快就成为我日常实际使用中最喜欢的东西之一。

请注意其中的 models.py 类型错误：在检查 api.py 时报告了该错误，而旧的每缓冲区视图会将其掉在地板上。 模式行中的 [project] 标记告诉您正在查看整个项目而不是单个文件。

通过 TRAMP 检查远程文件

这个很容易描述，而且老实说早该出现了：Flycheck 现在在 TRAMP 上运行检查器。 在远程主机上打开一个文件，检查器会在远程计算机上针对真实环境运行 - 之前它根本拒绝运行。 如果您通过 TRAMP 在服务器上或容器内编辑代码，仅这一点就值得升级。

还有更多

上述三位主角依赖于同一版本中的大量支持工作。 亮点：

  • Flycheck 现在可以应用修复程序。 嚯嚯！ f (flycheck-fix-error-at-point) 应用检查器建议的机器适用修复，C-c！ F 将缓冲区中的每个修复作为单个不可撤销的更改立即应用，并且可修复的错误会获得一个明显的边缘指示器 - 一个“可用修复”的小灯泡。 eslint --fix、cargo Clippy 的建议、ruff、shellcheck 和任何基于 SARIF 的检查器都带有这些修复程序，Flycheck 会解析并丢弃这些修复程序。
  • 错误列表进行了重大修改：按文件、检查器或级别对错误进行分组（并组合这些维度），折叠组，并通过顶部的条带用鼠标驱动所有错误。
  • 错误可以携带次要位置 - 重新定义背后的早期定义，Rust 生命周期错误背后的借用。 用 C-c 跳到他们那里！ j，它们显示在消息内联之后和错误列表中。
  • 当新的检查启动时，正在运行的检查会被中断（除非它已经取得了真正的进展），因此缓慢的检查器不再使 Flycheck 感觉缓慢，并且错误列表不再在每次光标移动时重新扫描其所有行。

变更日志中还有更多内容，但这就是它的形式。

把它们放在一起

如果您想要完整的现代设置 - 随处进行动态检查、内联诊断以及 LSP 服务器的诊断流经 Flycheck - 这里有一个 use-package 块可以将其全部打开：

(use-package flycheck
  :ensure t
  :hook ((after-init . global-flycheck-mode)
         ;; Show diagnostics inline, next to the code (Error Lens style)
         (after-init . global-flycheck-annotate-mode))
  :config
  ;; Report Eglot's LSP diagnostics through Flycheck
  (global-flycheck-eglot-mode 1))

更喜欢跳过 Eglot 并直接从 linter 自己的 LSP 服务器（RuboCop、Ruff、Biome、Harper）读取诊断信息？ 将最后一行替换为 (global-flycheck-lsp-mode 1)。 当您想要的只是诊断时，请使用本机检查器；当您还需要完整语言服务器的完成和悬停时，请使用 Eglot 桥接器。

升级中

大多数设置都会继续工作。 需要注意的一件事是：内置的 Flycheck-eglot-mode 重用了旧的第三方 Flycheck-eglot 软件包的名称，因此，如果您安装了该软件包，请在依赖内置模式之前将其卸载 - 否则两者定义相同的命令并发生冲突。

关于资金的一句话

让我在这里坦白一点，让我感到不舒服。 在我维护 Flycheck 的几年里，它的 OpenCollective 总共收入不到 300 美元。 个人捐款也没有完全发挥作用。 我这么说并不是为了让任何人感到内疚；这就是开源的日常现实。 受欢迎的项目需要大量的工作，而通常的回报是使用你帮助做得更好的东西所带来的安静的满足感。

不过，如果 Flycheck 可以节省您的时间（尤其是在工作中），请考虑通过 OpenCollective、GitHub 赞助商或 README 中链接的任何其他选项参与进来。 即使是很小的重复金额，乘以每天依赖这个东西的人，也会对我可以投入多少时间产生真正的影响。

结束语

即使是最小的人也可以改变未来的进程。 – 加拉德瑞尔

当我接手 Flycheck 时，我的动机很简单：让项目保持活力，让 Emacs 领域的竞争继续下去。 在很长一段时间内，这只不过意味着保持灯亮着。 这个版本是一段时间以来第一次真正取得重大进展，我对它的落地感到自豪 - 现代诊断用户体验、两种风格的一流 LSP 支持、项目范围的诊断和修复，同时保持人们喜爱的检查器模型。 称之为绝地归来。 我希望你会同意我在我打算做的事情上至少取得了一定的成功。

非常感谢所有测试、报告和推动这一点的人。 尝试一下 Flycheck-annotate-mode 和 Flycheck-lsp-mode，然后让我知道您的想法。

继续黑客攻击！
